# The aggregate tables {#sec-aggregate-tables}


::: {.cell}

:::


The aggregate tables are CSV files that open in any spreadsheet. They answer
most common questions without the vehicle table, and they have been built so
that results can be combined correctly. This chapter explains the three
families of table and the ideas common to all of them. @sec-table-catalogue
lists every file, and each family has a detailed report among the appendices.

## Ideas common to all the tables

### Grain

Each table has a **grain**: the combination of columns that identifies one
row. `mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv` has one row per year, postcode area,
body type and fuel group. Knowing the grain tells you what you can add up: you
can sum its rows over fuel groups to get totals by body type, or over postcode
areas to get national totals.

### Long and wide

Most tables come in **long** form, with one row per combination and one column
per measure, which is best for filtering and pivot tables. Some are also given
in **wide** form, with years (or categories) as columns, which is easier to
read and chart. They hold the same numbers.

### Counts and totals, not just averages

Where a table gives an average, it also gives the count and total it was
calculated from (for example `n_legit_mileage` and `total_legit_mileage`).

::: {.callout-important title="Pitfall: never average the averages"}
To get the average mileage of a group of rows, add up their totals and divide
by the sum of their counts. Taking the average of the rows' averages gives
each row equal weight, so a postcode area with 2,000 cars counts as much as one
with 2 million. @sec-examples-spreadsheet shows the right way in Excel.
:::

### Status rows

Postcode area columns include the statuses `unborn`, `unknown` and `dead` as
well as real areas, so a table's rows add up to every vehicle in the vehicle
table. For most analyses, **filter out the status rows** to keep the
vehicles observed in each year. Be aware that the share of vehicles that are
`unknown` grows towards the end of the series (@sec-lifecycle).

### Plausible mileage

Mileage is reported both in full and for plausible mileage only
(@sec-sources-linkage). Averages should normally use plausible mileage, as
the CARS reports do.

## Mileage tables

*Folder `tables/mileage/` · report: [Vehicles and mileage by postcode area](../reports/mileage_report.md)*

Vehicles and their annual mileage, for every MOT test class and body type.
The most useful single table is **`mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv`**, with
53,123 rows: for each year, postcode area (or status), DfT body
type and fuel group, it gives:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n_vehicles` | Vehicles |
| `n_with_mileage`, `n_legit_mileage` | Vehicles with a recorded, and with a plausible, mileage |
| `n_mileage_removed` | Vehicles whose mileage was judged implausible and removed |
| `total_mileage`, `total_legit_mileage` | Total miles, all recorded and plausible only |
| `n_negative_mileage`, `n_over_50k_mileage` | Vehicles with unusual mileages |
| `n_with_age`, `total_age` | For calculating average age |

The other mileage tables give the same information by age, by MOT test class
and by the fuel as DVSA supplied it, and the distribution of mileage in bands.

## Fleet profile tables

*Folder `tables/profile/` · report: [Fleet profile tables](../reports/fleet_profile_report.md)*

The make-up of the fleet in each year, for cars, light goods vehicles,
motorcycles and buses, by characteristics such as fuel, engine size, CO~2~
band, Euro standard, age band and (for cars) SMMT body type, with the vehicle
count and mean mileage of each. They come in long form
(`profile_categorical_by_year.csv`) and in four wide *analyses* per body type:

- **Analysis 1** (`a1_counts_*`): vehicles, years by characteristic;
- **Analysis 2** (`a2_mean_mileage_*`): mean mileage, years by characteristic;
- **Analyses 3 and 4**: the same, split by age band.

These tables cover Great Britain only (Northern Ireland is excluded) and count
a vehicle in a year only if it has a plausible mileage that year.

## Churn tables

*Folder `tables/churn/` · report: [Churn tables](../reports/churn_tables_report.md)*

The churn tables describe how the vehicles in each postcode area change: which
vehicles stay, which arrive from elsewhere or new, and which leave by moving
or by ceasing to be tested. They cover **MOT test class 4** vehicles: cars,
vans up to 3,000kg and small minibuses. They are organised in numbered sets:

| Set | Question |
|---|---|
| 0 | Where did each vehicle's first-use date come from? |
| 1 | Of the vehicles in an area in a reference year, how many are in the same area, a different one, dead or unborn in other years? |
| 2 | How many vehicles of each age, mileage, fuel and engine size are in each area each year, and what share stayed put? |
| 3 | What is each area's 2017 stock made of: stayers, arrivals and leavers either side? |
| 4 | Where are electric vehicles, where do they come from and where do they go? |
| 5 | Does moving area go with a change in mileage? |
| 6 | Which vehicles move between areas most often? |
| 7 | How many vehicles in each area are likely to fall foul of a Clean Air Zone, and which leave? |

: The churn table sets {#tbl-churn-sets}

::: {.callout-important title="Pitfall: a 'move' is a change of testing area"}
A vehicle counts as having moved when it is tested in a different postcode
area from the year before. That includes vehicles that changed garage without
changing address. Moves are also counted only between two years in which the
vehicle was observed, so a vehicle that disappears for a year and reappears
elsewhere has no move recorded.
:::
